passages.happening:
Paul looks straight at the council and says, “Brothers, I have conducted myself before God in all good conscience to this day” (verse 1). At this the high priest Ananias orders the men beside Paul to strike him on the mouth (verse 2).

Paul answers, “God will strike you, you whitewashed wall! You sit here to judge me according to the law, yet you yourself violate the law by commanding that I be struck” (verse 3). The bystanders say, “How dare you insult the high priest of God!” (verse 4). “Brothers,” Paul replies, “I was not aware that he was the high priest, for it is written: ‘Do not speak evil about the ruler of your people’” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
The council is the Sanhedrin, the Jewish high council in Jerusalem, led by the high priest. The Roman commander has called it together to find out what the charge against Paul really is (22:30).

The high priest is Ananias, the son of Nedebaeus. He is not the Ananias who baptized Paul in Damascus; the name was common. The Jewish historian Josephus tells of him. He was high priest for about a dozen years, from about AD 47; the years given for the end of his time in office differ. Josephus says his servants took by force the tithes that belonged to the ordinary priests, robbing the poorer priests of their share. He also says that years later, when the war against Rome broke out in AD 66, rebels burned his house and killed him, because he was seen as a friend of Rome. Paul's words, ‘God will strike you’, have often been read in the light of that end. Luke himself does not say so.

A ‘whitewashed wall’ was a wall that looked clean and solid because of its fresh coat of lime, while the wall underneath might be cracked and ready to fall. Paul is calling Ananias a man who looks like a judge of the law but breaks it. A man on trial had the right to be heard, and Ananias had him struck before any charge was proved.

Then Paul says he did not know he was speaking to the high priest. Readers take this in different ways, and Luke does not settle it. Some think Paul really did not recognise him. He had been away from Jerusalem for years, high priests changed often, and this was not a formal sitting where the high priest wore his robes; a few also point to signs that Paul's eyesight was poor (Galatians 4:15; 6:11). Others hear irony: a man who orders a prisoner struck against the law is not acting like a high priest, so how could Paul have known him for one? Many take it most simply: Paul spoke in anger, was told whom he had insulted, and at once accepted the rebuke of Scripture. On any of these readings Paul bows to God's law, even when it rebukes him.
passages.ot:
Paul quotes the Law of Moses. In the Berean Standard Bible's Exodus the command reads, “You must not blaspheme God or curse the ruler of your people” (Exodus 22:28); Acts gives the same law in slightly different words.

The whitewashed wall comes from Ezekiel. God spoke against false prophets who said ‘Peace’ when there was no peace, “whitewashing any flimsy wall that is built”, and warned “that it will fall” (Ezekiel 13:10-11). And the Law Ananias was meant to uphold said plainly, “You must not pervert justice” (Leviticus 19:15).
passages.asks: Paul spoke hot words to a man who had wronged him, and then, when Scripture rebuked him, he accepted it at once. Ask how you answer when you are treated unjustly, and how quickly you own it when your words go too far. And ask whose authority you find hardest to respect, and why.

passages.t: ‘I am a Pharisee’: the resurrection divides the council
passages.happening:
Paul knows that some of the council are Sadducees and others Pharisees. So he calls out, “Brothers, I am a Pharisee, the son of a Pharisee. It is because of my hope in the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial” (verse 6).

At once a dispute breaks out between the two groups, and the assembly is divided (verse 7). Luke explains: “the Sadducees say that there is neither a resurrection, nor angels, nor spirits, but the Pharisees acknowledge them all” (verse 8). Some scribes from the Pharisees stand up and argue, “We find nothing wrong with this man. What if a spirit or an angel has spoken to him?” (verse 9). The quarrel grows so violent that the commander fears Paul will be torn to pieces, and he sends soldiers to take him back into the barracks by force (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
The Sadducees were few and powerful. They were drawn from the priestly and wealthy families around the Temple. They held only to the written law, rejected the Pharisees' traditions, and said there is no resurrection, no angels and no spirits. The chief priests who led the council came mostly from their circle.

The Pharisees were the most popular of the Jewish groups. Most were not priests but lay people who tried to keep the law in ordinary life. They believed in the resurrection of the dead at the end of the age, when God would raise his people. Gamaliel, Paul's teacher, was one of them (5:34).

Was Paul's cry a clever trick to split his judges? Some readers see a tactic, and the quarrel that follows is real. But what Paul says is true and sincere. He was trained as a Pharisee, his father before him (Philippians 3:5). And the resurrection really was the centre of his message: he believed God had already raised one man, Jesus, as the first of the great raising the Pharisees hoped for. He will say the same before Felix (24:15, 21) and before King Agrippa (26:6-8). The council could not even agree on the hope his whole message rests on.

Notice the Pharisees' answer: ‘What if a spirit or an angel has spoken to him?’ They are not yet believers, but like Gamaliel before them they are cautious about fighting God (5:38-39).
passages.ot:
The hope of the resurrection rests on Israel's Scriptures. Daniel wrote, “And many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt” (Daniel 12:2). Isaiah promised, “Your dead will live; their bodies will rise” (Isaiah 26:19). Job said, “I know that my Redeemer lives, and in the end He will stand upon the earth” (Job 19:25).

The Sadducees held only to the written law, and Jesus answered them from it: God called himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob long after they had died (Exodus 3:6; Luke 20:37-38).
passages.asks: Paul named the one thing his whole life stood on: the hope that God raises the dead. Ask what you would say if you were asked, in a hostile room, why you believe what you believe. And ask whether the resurrection is the centre of your faith, or something at its edge.

passages.happening: The night after the council, Paul is back in the barracks, a prisoner with enemies on every side. “The following night the Lord stood near Paul and said, ‘Take courage! As you have testified about Me in Jerusalem, so also you must testify in Rome’” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
This is the hinge of the chapter. Paul has been beaten by a crowd, nearly flogged, struck on the mouth, and almost torn apart in the council, all in a few days. Everything looks like defeat.

Then the Lord himself stands beside him. He does not explain the suffering, and he does not promise that it will stop. He gives Paul two things: courage, and a future. Paul has long wanted to go to Rome. He wrote to the believers there that he hoped to visit them (Romans 1:10-13; 15:23-24). Now Jesus tells him he ‘must’ testify there. That small word ‘must’ is the one Luke uses for God's plan, as when Jesus said he must suffer (Luke 9:22).

The promise does not say how Paul will get to Rome. He will get there in chains, after two years in prison and a shipwreck. But from this night on, every delay in Acts is a delay on a road whose end has already been named.
passages.ot: ‘Take courage’ is the word God spoke to his people again and again. To Joshua he said, “Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go” (Joshua 1:9). Through Isaiah he said, “Do not fear, for I am with you; do not be afraid, for I am your God” (Isaiah 41:10). And to Jacob, alone at night far from home, he promised, “I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you” (Genesis 28:15).
passages.asks: The Lord did not take Paul out of prison that night. He stood beside him in it. Ask where you most need to hear ‘Take courage’ today. And ask whether you can trust a promise about where your road ends, even when you cannot see how you will get there.

passages.t: More than forty men swear to kill Paul
passages.happening: In the morning some men form a plot and bind themselves with an oath not to eat or drink until they have killed Paul (verse 12). More than forty of them are in it (verse 13). They go to the chief priests and elders and tell them about their oath (verse 14). Their plan: the council should ask the commander to bring Paul down again, “on the pretext of examining his case more carefully. We are ready to kill him on the way” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
Luke writes, ‘the Jews formed a conspiracy’ (verse 12). Who does he mean? Not the Jewish people, and not even the council as a whole, since part of the council had just said they found nothing wrong with Paul (verse 9). He means these more than forty men, and the chief priests and elders who agreed to help them. Paul himself, whom they want to kill, is a Jew, and so is the young man who will save him. The note on Acts 13:42-47 sets out how this site reads such phrases, and the note on Acts 2:22-28 explains how verses like this were later turned against the Jewish people, and why this site rejects that reading.

Their oath was a solemn one. The Greek verb means to put oneself under a curse: they called down God's curse on themselves if they ate or drank before Paul was dead. Luke says nothing more of them. We do not know what they did when the plot failed.

It was a time of violence in Judea. In these years, as the note on 21:37-40 says, the dagger-men called the sicarii killed their opponents in the crowds. A plan to ambush a prisoner on the road fitted the times. What makes it darker is that the plotters went to the chief priests, the keepers of the temple, and asked them to lie to the Roman commander so that a man could be murdered.
passages.ot:
God's law said, “You shall not murder” (Exodus 20:13), and it set a curse on anyone who “accepts a bribe to kill an innocent person” (Deuteronomy 27:25). Plotting the death of an innocent man is the plot the Psalms grieve over: “They conspire, they lurk, they watch my steps while they wait to take my life” (Psalm 56:6).

A rash oath is an old trap in Scripture. King Saul swore that no one would eat until he had taken revenge on his enemies, and the oath nearly cost his own son his life (1 Samuel 14:24, 44-45).
passages.asks: These men were so sure they were right that they swore not to eat until a man was dead, and leaders of the temple agreed to lie for them. Ask whether there is any cause you care about so much that you would let it excuse a lie or a cruelty. And ask how you can tell zeal for God from hatred dressed as zeal.

passages.happening:
But the son of Paul's sister hears about the ambush. He goes into the barracks and tells Paul (verse 16). Paul calls a centurion and asks him to take the young man to the commander (verse 17), and the centurion does (verse 18). The commander takes him by the hand, draws him aside and asks what he has to say (verse 19).

The young man tells him: “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul to the Sanhedrin tomorrow on the pretext of acquiring more information about him” (verse 20). Forty men are waiting in ambush, bound by an oath, ready now (verse 21). The commander sends him away with a warning: “Do not tell anyone that you have reported this to me” (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
This is the only time the New Testament mentions any of Paul's family. He had a sister, and her son was in Jerusalem, perhaps living there or studying there as Paul once had. We know nothing more about them: not their names, nor whether they believed in Jesus. But one young man's courage saved his uncle's life. He went alone into a Roman fortress to warn him.

‘The Jews have agreed’, he says. The young man is himself a Jew, speaking of the plotters and the leaders who were helping them, not of his own people as a whole. The note on Acts 13:42-47 sets out how this site reads such phrases.

The Roman commander is shown in a good light here. He takes the young man ‘by the hand’, a kind gesture, listens in private, and believes him. And he acts at once. Luke shows that God's promise of verse 11 is kept through ordinary people: a nephew who overheard, a centurion who carried a message, a soldier who listened.
passages.ot:
God has often saved his people through someone young or unnoticed. A young Israelite girl, a captive in a foreign house, told Naaman's wife about the prophet in Samaria (2 Kings 5:2-3). Mordecai learned of a plot to kill the king and passed it on through Esther, and the plot failed (Esther 2:21-23).

The Psalms praise the God who frustrates the schemes of the wicked: “The LORD frustrates the plans of the nations; He thwarts the devices of the peoples” (Psalm 33:10).
passages.asks: A young man whose name we do not know walked into a fortress to save a life. Ask whether there is a word of warning or truth you should carry to someone, even at a cost. And notice how God kept his promise to Paul: not by a miracle this time, but through a family member and a soldier. Ask whether you look for God's help only in the dramatic, and miss it in the ordinary.

passages.t: An escort, and Claudius Lysias's letter
passages.happening:
The commander calls two centurions and orders a force ready by the third hour of the night: “two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen, and two hundred spearmen” (verse 23). Horses are to be provided for Paul, to bring him safely to Felix the governor (verse 24).

He writes a letter (verse 25), which Luke gives in full. “Claudius Lysias, To His Excellency, Governor Felix: Greetings” (verse 26). The man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed when he came with his troops and rescued him, “For I had learned that he is a Roman citizen” (verse 27). He brought him before their council (verse 28) and found that the charges were about their own law, with nothing deserving death or prison (verse 29). Learning of a plot, he sent the man at once, and he has told the accusers to bring their case to Felix (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
The third hour of the night was about nine in the evening. Four hundred and seventy men, to guard one prisoner. The commander takes the threat seriously. A Roman citizen murdered while in his care would mean trouble for him in Rome.

Now we learn his name: Claudius Lysias. The name fits a man who took the emperor's name, Claudius, when he bought his citizenship (22:28), though that is an inference.

His letter follows the ordinary form of letters in that world: the sender, the person addressed, ‘Greetings’, and then the business. But read it beside what has happened, and it shades the truth in his own favour. He says he rescued Paul because he had learned Paul was a Roman citizen. In fact he arrested Paul to stop a riot (21:33), bound him in chains, and was about to have him flogged, and he learned that Paul was a citizen only when Paul spoke up on the whipping post (22:25-29). The flogging and the chains are left out. Luke lets the reader see the gap without comment. It is how officials often write about themselves. When the letter says Paul ‘was seized by the Jews’, it means the crowd in the temple, stirred up by some Jews from Asia (21:27); the note on Acts 13:42-47 sets out how this site reads such phrases.

Yet the letter also says something that matters for the rest of Acts: there was ‘no charge worthy of death or imprisonment’. A Roman officer, with no reason to favour Paul, finds him innocent. Luke will record the same verdict from Festus and Agrippa (25:25; 26:31-32), as Pilate three times found no basis for a charge against Jesus (Luke 23:4, 14, 22).

Felix, the governor of Judea, appears in the next chapter.
passages.ot:
God's law asked for honest testimony: “You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor” (Exodus 20:16). The Proverbs prize the honest report: “Truthful lips endure forever, but a lying tongue lasts only a moment” (Proverbs 12:19).

The large escort for one prisoner recalls Elisha's servant, who saw an enemy army around the city until his eyes were opened and he saw “that the hills were full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha” (2 Kings 6:17). Here the horses are Roman, and God uses them.
passages.asks: Claudius Lysias told the truth about Paul's innocence and bent the truth about himself. Ask whether, when you tell a story you are part of, you quietly leave out what makes you look bad. And notice that God protected Paul through a proud, self-serving officer. Ask whether you can see God at work even through people whose motives are mixed.

passages.t: By night to Antipatris and Caesarea
passages.happening:
The soldiers follow orders and take Paul by night as far as Antipatris (verse 31). The next day the foot soldiers go back to the barracks and leave the horsemen to go on with him (verse 32). At Caesarea the horsemen hand the letter to the governor and present Paul to him (verse 33).

Felix reads the letter and asks which province Paul is from. Learning that he is from Cilicia (verse 34), he says, “I will hear your case when your accusers arrive.” Then he orders Paul to be kept under guard in Herod's Praetorium (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
Antipatris lay on the road down from the hills of Judea to the coastal plain, roughly forty miles from Jerusalem by the usual reckoning. It was the edge of the dangerous hill country. Once there, the foot soldiers could go back, and the horsemen could cover the open plain to Caesarea quickly.

Caesarea was the city on the coast where the Roman governors lived. Herod the Great had built it, with a harbour and a palace. The ‘Praetorium’ was the governor's headquarters, here Herod's old palace. Paul is a prisoner, but held in the governor's own residence rather than a common jail.

Felix asks which province Paul is from. Luke does not say why. Perhaps he was checking whether the case was his to hear. Either way, he decides to hear it himself, once the accusers arrive.

So Paul leaves Jerusalem for the last time in Acts. He came to bring a gift and to worship. He leaves at night, surrounded by soldiers, to save his life. Luke does not tell us that he ever saw the city again.
passages.ot:
Caesarea, a Gentile city of governors, is where Peter first preached to a Gentile household (Acts 10). Now Paul will bear witness there before rulers, as Jesus had told his followers: “you will stand before governors and kings as witnesses to them” (Mark 13:9; also Luke 21:12). The Psalms carry the same hope: “I will speak of Your testimonies before kings, and I will not be ashamed” (Psalm 119:46).

God's care for a man fleeing by night echoes David's escape from Saul, when his wife let him down through a window (1 Samuel 19:11-12).
passages.asks: Paul left Jerusalem by night, a prisoner, and it looked like the end of his work there. It was the start of his witness before governors and kings. Ask whether something that feels like being carried away from your plans might be the road God's promise is taking. And ask how you live in the waiting place, as Paul now must, ‘under guard’.
